It is said that the essence of the generative cause (*janaka-hetu*) does not possess the three characteristics (*tri-lakṣaṇa*). However, because it expresses the meaning of the three characteristics, it is designated as "having the three characteristics" by virtue of that which is expressed (*vācya*).

This intends to mean that the expressed meaning (*artha*) underlying the expressive words (*vācaka*), and the object of cognition (*ālambana*) underlying the cognizing subject (*ālambaka*), both possess the three characteristics, such as "being a property of the subject" (*pakṣadharmatva*).
Yet, for those who oppose and challenge [the argument], the actual generative cause—the cognition—does not truly possess them.

The three characteristics (trilakṣaṇa) are merely designated as the "cause" (hetu). It is said that the cause possesses the three characteristics; because they are spoken of in accordance with their respective aspects, it is stated that each has its own three characteristics.
Regarding the commentary’s point that the basis of the cause (hetvāśraya) runs through all three distinct locations:
The three specific [factors] are the subject (dharmin) of the thesis and the similar and dissimilar examples (dṛṣṭānta). These three constitute the basis for the reason (hetu).
Although the dissimilar class (vipakṣa) does not accord with it, it is nevertheless called a "basis" by way of contrast.
The Commentary states: "Therefore, these two dharmas are both distinct attributes (*viśeṣa*) upon a dharma that possesses them.
This means that the properties of impermanence (*anityatā*) and being produced (*kṛtakatva*) are the distinct attributes upon the dharma of sound.
The Commentary states that when a general term is applied to a particular instance, it refers to their being combined and inseparable;
this constitutes the general thesis (*sāmānya-pakṣa*). When the bases of these two are distinct, they are termed "particular" (*viśeṣa*).

Since a particular is already a single part within the whole, the particular is also spoken of by means of the general term, just as the lapels and sleeves must first form a complete garment before they can be called such. Only...
When burning a *shān* (a robe), one also says "burning the garment," because the term refers to the entire assembly including the sash.
Regarding the statement that "the phenomenon (*dharma*) possesses both smoke and fire":
this means that just as form (*rūpa*) and so forth constitute the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), that very nature is the phenomenon; it is not a case of presenting [the subject] first.

This refers to the existence of phenomena. However, it is for the purpose of establishing this associated entity that this is said: when there is fire and smoke on a mountain, it is called "association.

As for the statement in the commentary, "There are things not established [here], which are all revealed by means of establishment," it means that while certain entities are not explicitly posited here, they are nonetheless made manifest through the process of logical establishment.
The commentary states: If the reason were to pervade the entire thesis, there would be a principle for what is to be established; yet it has not been so established.

If this were not the case, then it would not be an establishment at all. Regarding the two types of "one-part" [reasons], whether they belong to oneself or to another, when combined with the three types of "one-part" reasons, they constitute the "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*) fallacy due to doubt.
The question asks whether non-existence has no substance. If one answers by discussing existence and non-existence, that constitutes a definitive resolution rather than hesitation.

One should look to what follows in the section on "hesitation" (pre) to see the basis [of this]. The reason it does not say that non-existence lacks substance is that, if it lacked substance, it would not serve as a basis.
This is why it is said that there is only the substance (*tattva*).
As for the commentary’s failure to mention the two different names for the pot among the synonyms,
its intention is to state that what is produced upon the sound is precisely what is produced upon the pot.
The commentary states that because [the four] "constantly abide," are "firm and solid," and "unchanging," all four are eternal.
This explains the concealment of the term "eternal. To speak of "transmigration" is to conceal the term "impermanent.
The commentary further notes that the aforementioned faults apply to the three preceding phrases.

The three characteristics of the reason (*hetu*) constitute the three propositions. Furthermore, it is stated that "each characteristic" refers to their meaning (*artha*), not their substantial essence (*svabhāva*).
Regarding the phrase "all three established [factors] are missing":
this refers to the one reason and two examples which constitute the means of proof (*sādhana*).
The Commentary states: Thus, there are three sets of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
This means that each of the three characteristics takes its turn as the primary subject, and through their mutual presence and absence, the three [sets] are established.
As for the "one set of two propositions," this refers to the case where three [characteristics] are absent while the remaining one is not absent.
Regarding the statement in the commentary that "because the meaning of the reason [is established], there is no fault of the latter two types of non-establishment (asiddha)":

first, as for "non-establishment of the locus" (*āśrayāsiddha*), this constitutes a division of the property-bearer (*dharmin*). Since the reason would lack a locus, it carries the meaning of being "without a reason."
The remainder may be fully understood as appropriate by consulting the treatise (*śāstra*).
Regarding the statement that "only the *lakṣaṇa-viruddha* (contradiction of characteristics) exists," this refers to the four *api-śabdāḥ* (the term 'also' or 'and').
As for the mention of the "five indeterminate [factors]," this refers to the six indeterminate factors (*aniyata*) with the exception of the *lakṣaṇa-samagra* (complete set of characteristics).

Because it contradicts the certainty [of the definition], six of the nine propositions are subsumed under faults, while the remaining four are not established. First, the three characteristics are mutually contradictory;
thus, they are not subsumed within the nine propositions.
The commentary answers that because the reason (*hetu*) is proximate to the thesis (*pakṣa*), it establishes [the latter] and so forth;

as for the indication of its conformity or opposition, the meaning here is this: since the reason is proximate to the thesis, among the nine types of reasons, the presence of the first characteristic is what constitutes conformity.
If the first characteristic were absent, there would be the fault of the four types of non-establishment (*asiddha*); therefore, the four types of non-establishment are not mentioned. Furthermore...

The *Jie* (Exegesis) speaks only of the "pervasive reason" (*vyāpya-hetu*) because it successfully establishes the thesis (*pakṣa*). Thus, it does not mention the four types of "unestablished" (*asiddha*) reasons.

Furthermore, because the establishment of the "similar instance" (*sapakṣa*) is remote, it merely indicates what is "concordant" (*anuloma*) and what is "discordant" (*pratiloma*). "Concordant" refers to the five types of "uncertain" (*anaikāntika*) reasons;

"discordant" refers to the two types of "contradictory" (*viruddha*) reasons. Based on this, all other cases are subsumed without exception; there is no need to further state the remaining three types of contradiction or the definitive [reasons].

This is an error regarding the fixed [classification]. Furthermore, as for the mention of "conformity and opposition" (*anuloma-viloma*) and so forth: among the nine propositions, six are conforming, while the remaining are all opposing metaphors (*dṛṣṭānta*).
Since they do not share the sense of being directly established like a logical reason (*hetu*), they are described as conforming and opposing.
Regarding the commentary’s response concerning the assertion of the identity or difference of the thesis (*pakṣa*) based on the presence or absence of the reason (*hetu*):
because the reason exists in one instance, this is stated to be the same as the thesis and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). This can be understood from the cited text.
The Commentary states: "If he does not admit that sound is a property-possessor (*dharmin*), it also constitutes a dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*).

Only when both the proponent and the opponent do not admit [a certain thing] does it constitute a dissimilar instance; it is not merely the case for the other [the opponent]. Regarding the thesis (*pakṣa*) being established, if the other [the opponent] does not admit it, it is designated as a dissimilar instance.
The commentary does not mean that the "dharma" and the "possessor of dharma" mentioned in those words do not exist elsewhere;
rather, its intent is that while there may simply be no "proven dharma" in other instances (vipakṣa), it is not necessary for both [the dharma and its possessor] to be absent in all other instances.
The commentary answers: "That the nature of sound is impermanent has the meaning of cessation (*nirodha*), while the essence of *samāpatti* has the meaning of arising (*utpāda*).
This serves as proof for the meaning of impermanence. However, this is not a separate dharma that can be expressed by words.

Yet, just as a tortoise's hair cannot be treated in the same way [as a real entity], it is not non-existent. Since there is neither impermanence nor permanence, it is subsumed under the category of "difference" (*anya*) and is not [non-existent].
Regarding the "Shared Category" (俱句): The Commentary states that both of these two masters hold the view that there is "a portion of all internal and external things as having different natures.

This means that either a portion is internal or external, or else all internal and external things are together [of different natures]. Furthermore, regarding what is called "one essence and many essences," these two...
There are two types of accepted phenomena (*dharma*): first, those that posit all phenomena as existing, such as the *tathatā* (suchness) of the Mahāyāna;
second, those in which each phenomenon possesses its own specific designating sound (*śabda*), such as the "cessation through grasping" (*upādāya-nirodha*) of the Sarvāstivāda.
The commentary (*śāstra*) also establishes emptiness, selflessness, and so forth according to their respective applications, rather than taking everything [literally].
The intent clarifies that the reason (*hetu*) does not merely establish that "sound is permanent," nor does it generally establish all properties of the subject (*dharmin*).

As for the phrase "each meaning is established individually," this can be understood through the example of "indefinite" (*anaikāntika*), just as with names. Regarding the "reason of action" (*kāryahetu*) among its various types...
[The term] "turns" [is used] because it understands the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "If it were not identical, it would differ from the general thesis (*pakṣa*); that which is equal to it is called a 'dharma'":
the intended meaning is that the dharma belonging to the proponent's thesis is called a "dharma" because it is identical to that [thesis]; it does not differ from it.

As for the "thesis" (*pakṣa*): it merely takes the jar and impermanence as being inseparable; this is similar to the general category of that thesis, which can be described as having specific varieties.
Furthermore, the commentary states: "This 'produced nature' (*kṛtaka*) is not the general [property] established."
That which is established as the "probandum" (*sādhya*) is itself the "probans" (*sādhana*). Therefore, the commentary concludes by stating: "Because the probandum and the probans are distinct.

Regarding the passage in the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) from "excluding the thesis (*pakṣa*)" up to "in the collection of existence and non-existence, there are these dharmas that are both commonly accepted and not commonly accepted": [this refers to the fact that while the subject may be commonly accepted, the attributes predicated of it may be either].
This intention applies universally because it establishes both the positions of existence and non-existence; thus, the example applies to both.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "that which is mutually accepted or not accepted within this very [position]": within this position, all produced things are mutually accepted, whereas impermanent phenomena are not mutually accepted.

The Commentary states: If, at that time, the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa) established were not of a single kind but were [multiple] opponents, then because they would be the very dissimilar instances of what is being established, the dissimilar instances would not be distinct from what is being established.
Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* that "that which possesses the property to be proven (*sādhyadharmin*) should be taken as the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*)," the intended meaning is this:

since the probandum lacks such a dissimilar instance, there must, according to that school's tenet, exist another entity that is a real dharma, which is distantly distinguished from it by its being non-existent (*asat*).

The Commentary states: "If [it is argued that] the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is the thesis (*pakṣa*), then since it is not a cause capable of producing [an effect], there would be nothing upon which it could depend.
This means that a cause must not depend on a non-existent entity (*abhāva*). Question:

Within the context of a non-existent thesis, if the phenomenon (*dharma*) itself exists, and since existence (*bhāva*) is that upon which the produced depends, can the non-existent thesis then be established? Answer: Although this specific fault does not apply, there are yet other faults.

There is another fault. Someone asks: "If one posits that there is no cause for an existent phenomenon (*dharmin*), does this not establish two contradictory positions? Furthermore, is it not the fault of the locus (*āśraya*) being unestablished?
The answer is: This is not such a fault. Therefore, we do not say that there is no cause for an existent phenomenon. An existent phenomenon (*dharmin*) can be either existent or non-existent.
When one asks whether there is no cause for an existent phenomenon, the fact that it is either existent or non-existent is not a fault; how much less so when there is a cause for it?
There is a thesis (pakṣa). How could it be that there is no fault of lacking a basis? Answer: Because the reason (hetu) is established, there is no fault of the thesis lacking a basis.
If the reason is not established, then there is no basis; this itself is the fault.
Regarding the statement, "Since the causes of diligence and vigor are the same as those of the 'produced' (*kṛtaka*), one should say 'also' (*api*)," the intended meaning is as follows:

All other meanings are the same as those of the "produced," yet this cause additionally includes "not exceeding" (*atigamana*) and "not desiring" (*anabhilāṣa*). This is to distinguish it from the previous causes;
therefore, "non-pervasive" (*avyāpin*) should also be added.
The commentary states: "Regarding the point that the meaning is accepted as being identical to the sound [itself], [the reason] 'being produced' [proves] impermanence.
Question: Since the opponent has already accepted impermanence, is this not the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*)? Answer:
Because the opponent first does not accept it, and only accepts it once the logical reason (*hetu*) has been established, there is no fallacy of proving what is already established."

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “It clarifies that the impermanence of sound is also determined by its conformity with the similar instance (sapakṣa) based on the reason,” the intended meaning is as follows:
Because it conforms to the reason present upon that jar, which serves as the similar instance, it is definitively established that sound is impermanent, just like [the jar].
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "the same class as the jar":
although this is a common example (*sādhāraṇadṛṣṭānta*), it refers to the opponent as "one's own" (*sva*).
The commentary further states: "To speak of a different school and a different reason means to establish another meaning separately; the 'same class' (*sapakṣa*) [is established] in this way."
The phrase "different thesis and different reason" means that one establishes a distinct thesis and reason.
As for the example of "the four branches" and so forth, it refers to the four divisions of an army.
Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* that "the ten bases of form (*rūpāyatana*) are certainly not substantially existent" up to "all [objects] external to the Buddha are attained by the Buddha":

first, among those ten bases of form, the five consciousnesses, the mental consciousness immediately following them, the meditative mind, the five objects (*viṣaya*) as perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and the ten bases of form as perceived by the Buddha’s mind—all these are substantially existent as objects of direct perception. Excluding these...

All that is clarified here is understood through inference (*anumāna*) as being substantially existent dharmas. Question: Why do the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) and the untainted mind (*anāsravacitta*) of the Two Vehicles not take these as their objects?

Answer: The knowledge of others' minds takes the other's mind itself as its object; because the untainted mind takes ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) as its object, it does not take the faculties (*indriya*) as its object.
Regarding the statement that the commentary cites its own [teachings] as proof for those who do not yet believe others:
this means that while one intends to cause others to have faith by citing one's own sacred teachings, to instead personally violate and turn away from them is a minor transgression.
Regarding the statement, "Because when one confronts an opponent to present one's own tenet (zong), there will inevitably be conflict," the intended meaning is as follows:
To oppose another and accord with oneself is what is called a "tenet" (zong). Therefore, to oppose the teachings of another does not constitute a fault.
"Embracing a rabbit" (huaitu) refers to concealment. This is the intended meaning behind the statement that there is a rabbit within the moon.
Regarding the "various forms of the Bodhisattvas in their final bodies" mentioned in the *Shujian* [Commentary] on the various Hīnayāna schools:
according to the tenets of those schools, the body of Śākyamuni is considered his final body. Prior to the thirty stages of mind (*triṃśac-citta*), there is... [text fragment].

Regarding the "perception of malice" (*vyāpādavitarka*), it gives rise to defiled bodily and vocal actions. Those [actions] are admitted by us to be subsumed under the first three [bases], because they are not subsumed under visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), just like the eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*).
These two—the reason and the example—are what we of the Sarvāstivāda school ourselves admit; therefore, in the commentary below:

Regarding the contradiction with the determined specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the property-possessor (*dharmin*) in the former case, and the contradiction with the specific characteristic of the property (*dharma*) in the latter case—both are erroneous.

In the Mahāyāna, the indirect object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is not necessarily separated from the cognizing consciousness; it is distinguished [from the direct object] by means of an inference based on its arising.

The commentary further states: "Regarding the point that the common example also suffers from the fallacy of the unestablished probandum (*sādhyāprasiddhi*), up to the phrase 'neither identical nor separate':

it is commonly accepted that the principle of cause and effect regarding consciousness is neither identical nor separate; yet now you claim they are definitely separate, which means the probandum within the example is unestablished.

Furthermore, as for the mention of 'the wisdom that accomplishes activities' (*krtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) and so forth, this is an objection based on our own school’s tenets; in our school, the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*)..."

And the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) is likewise not separate from it. Question: It is reasonable that the objective aspect is close [to consciousness], but how can this be said of the substance (*bimba*), which is distant?

Answer: Because the substance possesses the objective aspect, the aspect does not depart from it. Furthermore, when it is said that there is a sense of separation, the intention is to state that there is a contradiction in mere words;

how could it be that they are definitively not separate? This serves to clarify the meaning of their non-separation. Question: In the Mahāyāna, since the substance and the objective aspect are not separate from consciousness...

How can there be cognition of separation? Answer: In terms of functional capacity (*śakti*), that which is proximate is cognition through contact (*saṃyoga-jñāna*); that whose functional capacity is remote is the meaning of cognition of separation.
Question: According to the Mahāyāna, what constitutes the certainty of separation? Answer: Because the sense organ (*indriya*) gives rise to consciousness (*vijñāna*), it is indeed certain.
This is the aforementioned fault of "certainty"; one cannot say it is not certain and yet not separated.
The Commentary states: "This is said to be a contradiction with one's own definitive words" in order to exclude hesitation.
The Commentary asks: "If one says 'I am thought' and so forth, how can one establish that the self exists?"

Regarding this question: "If, prior to this, the name of this dharma is not established as that which is to be distinguished (*viśeṣya*), then since no dharma is admitted in any state whatsoever, how can 'acquisition' (*prāpti*) be established?
[The *Śū* states: "If there is something to be distinguished, then there is no fault. Furthermore, it says: "As for those things such as the signifier (*vācaka*) that follow [the signified]," etc.

The intention is this: since there is that which expresses and that which is expressed, when the meaning is established, it is formulated in a concise manner; thus, the aforementioned fault does not occur.
Otherwise, the object of qualification would fail to be established.
The commentary addresses two faults above.

Regarding the first fault mentioned below, taking the initial statement as erroneous, it should instead be placed where the subsequent statement stands. As for the subsequent fault, it should be stated that "the basis of the initial thesis is unestablished.
Thus, one should state that while there is the first fault regarding the predicate (*viśeṣya*), there is also [a fault regarding] the subject (*viśeṣaṇa*). One should state the subject.
Since there is no "distinguisher" (viśeṣaṇa) that exists apart from the "thing to be distinguished" (viśeṣya), the commentary states that the initial and final characters are transposed.

Regarding the commentary’s point that "the thesis is not named after its substratum (āśraya) or its superstratum (āśrita)," this is because the general thesis (pakṣa) is neither the thing to be distinguished nor the distinguisher; therefore, it is not the substratum.

The commentary states: "Regarding the point that 'the established [property] and the name of the substratum are not yet definitively determined, yet for the time being, one may distinguish the nature of inseparability as the established property without assigning it the names of the substratum or the supported;
this should likewise be without fault. The intent of the commentary is that if something is not included among those accepted as real, it occurs only within the systems of other schools."
Within the four great elements, it is not that there is no reality; yet, while not being real, it is also real—a distinction [between] the subtle and the coarse.

As for the commentary stating "contradicting another's manifest [view], but not contradicting one's own teaching": this refers to cases where one’s position conflicts with the explicit assertions of others, yet does not conflict with the tenets of one's own school.

As stated in the *Abhidharmadīpa* regarding the Vaiśeṣika school: "The three elements of earth, water, and fire are not visible to the eye," because that school claims they are indeed perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
The commentary states:
"This would contradict one's own direct perception and involve the fallacy of the unestablished qualifier (*viśeṣya-asiddha*)."

According to the Mahāyāna, with respect to all that exists—excluding the eye-faculty that is the object of the meditative mind of a Buddha—I accept this on the basis of my own tenet, because the meditative mind takes the eyes and so forth as its objects;
however, other schools do not accept that the self is these two.
Regarding the commentary’s statement that there are four sets of four propositions:
the first set of four excludes the ninth; the second set of four excludes the third; and within the fourth set of four, the first is excluded.
Regarding the commentary’s further point that what is stated in this treatise contradicts direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and involves four fallacies, and so forth:
This refers to the discussion of methodological errors within the treatise (*śāstra*).
In the commentaries (*vṛtti*), there are cases involving "self," "other," and "both.
"Both" means that it contradicts both self and other; "not both" means that it does not contradict either self or other.
The commentary (śūtra) uses the phrase "with one's own manifestation as the counterpart.
In this context, it should be stated that two [of the four] sets of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) are fully established, while one part is partially established.
Regarding the commentary’s mention of "either the same or different schools":
This reason is identical to the "reason that exists in the dissimilar class" (*vipakṣa*).
The *Śū* (Commentary) states: "A non-existent reason cannot depend on a real entity (*dharmin*), for a real entity encompasses both existence and non-existence.

Elsewhere, it further states: "A non-existent reason cannot establish existence. This latter point regarding the establishment of existence refers to the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*). This...

Regarding the reason given—that it is not included within the Buddha’s word—it is asked: "Do you also admit that the *Jñānaprasthāna* is not the Buddha’s word? The answer is: "For the time being, we set aside the *Jñānaprasthāna*.

There are subsequent difficulties such as the 'difficulty of successive existences' (*paścāt-paścād-bhava-doṣa*) and so forth. Furthermore, regarding the statement that the *Jñānaprasthāna* itself admits it was spoken by the Buddha:
this cites a portion of their own school's position to formulate an "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*) fallacy. Moreover, it says "the other minor... [text fragment].

Because that which is "mounted" is precisely what is excluded. Regarding those who assert this according to one part of that school—namely, all other Hīnayāna schools and Mahāyānists—they collectively accept that the *Jñānaprasthāna* is a compilation of the Buddha’s words, yet it was not spoken by the Buddha himself, nor is it included within the six *Pādas* of the non-Buddhists.

Therefore, it is said that both parties agree on its being "extremely established" (ubhayasiddha) as something not subsumed under the Buddha, and thus not the Buddha’s word. As for that which is not the Buddha’s word:

This refers to the six *pāda* treatises of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and so forth. Furthermore, it is said that these are not included within the Buddha’s word (*buddhavacana*). This statement means they are not the Buddha’s word;
it does not mean that the names of the non-Buddhist *ṣatpāda* treatises themselves are not the Buddha’s word. That which is the Buddha’s word is not definitively fixed by the Buddha himself.

The commentary states that because even a single portion [of the opponent's position] is invalidated for both parties, it reveals that those who follow the *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna* and those of the Mahāyāna school alike do not admit that such [a teaching] is not the Buddha’s word or is not included within the canon.
How could you, a follower of the Mahāyāna, admit that it is not the Buddha’s word and is not included? How could you, a follower of the Mahāyāna, admit that it is not the Buddha’s...?

Regarding the phrase "both [sides] equally fail to establish" (*ubhayāsiddha*): prior to the text, the Great One (the opponent) has already introduced the cognition of production (*utpādajñāna*) as being indeterminate;

this serves as the reason (*hetu*). Taking the cognition of production as it is apprehended within the subject (*dharmin*) as the thesis (*pakṣa*), this reason fails to be established for both parties.
This reason, with respect to the cognition of production, lacks the sequential consistency [required]. The intended meaning is that the previous [argument] was based on what is not the Buddha’s word.

Regarding the statement "it is not included": it is not subsumed under the speech of non-Buddhists. Since it exists within the *Jñānaprasthāna* and is subsequently established as the word of the Buddha, its presence in the *Jñānaprasthāna* does not contradict [the claim that it is not subsumed by non-Buddhist teachings].

The commentary states that for those who claim to be "wise ones" (*jñānin*) according to their own [Mahāyāna] tenets—such as those who accept one part of the Mahāyāna while rejecting another, or those for whom both [aspects] are established as ultimate within the Mahāyāna itself—it is not said that these are not the word of the Buddha simply because they are not included among the six *pāda* treatises of the non-Buddhists; this differs from the meaning explained previously. This is so.
The term "single cause" contains these two meanings; as their perspectives differ, they each provide a refutation accordingly.
As the commentary states: "For example, one who is certain about the horn but has doubt regarding the ox."
This refers to the case where the object to be qualified (*viśeṣya*) is certain, while the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is subject to doubt.

For example, someone seeing a horn through a wall may be certain it is a cow's horn, yet remain in doubt as to whether it is a bull’s horn or something worn by a cow. Or, one might be certain of smoke on a mountain but have doubt regarding fire.

In these cases, the qualifier is certain while the object to be qualified is uncertain; for instance, when one says "there is fire under the smoke," the fire is established because one perceives the fire itself, which is certain.
Regarding the presentation of the thesis (*pratijñā*) to an opponent: one naturally gives rise to doubt beforehand, thinking that smoke is a characteristic (*liṅga*) of fire.
Now, since the thesis is presented to an opponent, doubt arises regarding the smoke itself; one does not give rise to doubt regarding the fire.
The commentary states: "If both [parties] equally doubt, this constitutes 'failure to establish for both' (*ubhaya-asiddha*), 'established for both' (*ubhaya-siddha*), and so forth.
The term "both" (*ubhaya*) in the first instance contains two meanings: namely, the distinction between subject and object, and the combination of self and other.

The term "both" in the latter instance likewise refers to the distinction between subject and object, as well as the combination of self and other; "neither being established for both" refers to both self and other.

Regarding the commentary’s previous statement that "the thesis (*pakṣa*) appears to be merely the locus (*āśraya*), but since it is said that there is no meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) and yet there is a substantial entity (*sattva*), [the reason] is unestablished due to doubt," the intended meaning is as follows:
The previous [statement] was based on the absence of a substantial entity and did not mention unestablishment due to doubt, because doubt and certainty are distinct.
Now, because it is said that there *is* a substantial entity, there is doubt and thus unestablishment. "You" (*yǒu*) means a dog; "yù" (*yù*) means before. It is like a dog.
The son was walking ahead. Upon reaching a fork in the road, he hesitated while waiting for others; thus, the present hesitation is also like this.
Because it encounters such indeterminate things as clouds, smoke, and dew, it is called "hesitation" (yū-i).
The commentary answers: "Although the reason possesses three characteristics, if only the first characteristic is present, it is termed 'unestablished' (*asiddha*).

This is an illustration. The phrase "possessing [the other characteristics] according to other schools" refers to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth. The phrase "combining two to establish a thesis" refers to...

This commentary explains that the term "established thesis" (*siddha-pakṣa*) is obtained by excluding what is not established; conversely, one obtains the name "unestablished" (*asiddha*) by excluding this [established] thesis.

As for the statement that the meaning of "establishing the thesis" is remote, it is because the traditional explanation states that the thesis must possess [the five members]. However, the name is not fixed. Regarding "contradiction," it refers to the latter two characteristics of the reason (*hetu*).
The Commentary states, "All that exists is not shared," intending to clarify that the term "all that exists" refers to all non-shared causes.
Regarding the phrase in the Commentary, "like wild grass on a mountain":

This analogy can be understood. It clarifies the meaning of the "uncommon reason" (*asādhāraṇa-hetu*). Although it does not belong to either the similar class (*sapakṣa*) or the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), it nevertheless possesses the quality of establishing one of the two theses.
How is this measured? For example, consider the thesis that sound is eternal. That which is heard [i.e., sound] is entirely absent from a pot;
although empty space is a member of the similar class for the thesis, it is a property distinct from the reason. If one were to take [this as the reason]:
That jar serves as a counter-example (*vipakṣa*). By way of contrast, it reveals that which is permanent and that which is impermanent; therefore, it is called "indeterminate" (*anaikāntika*).
Regarding the passage in the Commentary stating, "The son of the detached one [Vatsagotra]... I have life," etc.:
because he is a descendant of that lineage, the term "son" used here refers to one who lacks life and cannot grow, just like a gourd vine.
Because it is difficult [to obtain] melons and the like from atop trees, it is said that they have no life; conversely, those that can be obtained are said to have life. [The commentary states:
"However, although both cases are obtainable, there is a contradiction in their respective meanings."
This means that there is a single object which, being contrary to that [subject], cannot possibly coexist with it; therefore, this constitutes doubt.
As for the commentary’s statement: "That which is produced is always unified, while that which produces is always free from multiplicity."

The mind is capable of producing [results], yet all possess parents; the child produced is singular. Even down to the smallest portion of earth, the child is a single atom (*paramāṇu*), while its parents may be many.
Regarding the question of whether the atomic child does not exceed the magnitude of its cause: it does indeed exceed by one.
"Parents are the primary enemy. The commentary explains that within the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, this refutes the view that [the parents] are applicable to both [types of enemies].
The sub-commentary states that this is not the same as the Vaiśeṣika position regarding the nature of sound.
This briefly distinguishes between the two schools regarding the nature of sound (*śabda*). What is their meaning? Furthermore, according to the two theories of sound, there are two types of sound:

first, that which is like the *tathatā* (suchness) of the Mahāyāna; second, that which is subsumed under cessation (*nirodha*) in the Sarvāstivāda school. Now, as for the nature of sound in the Vaiśeṣika school:

Identity and difference are not established as separate categories; rather, they are simply the nature of identity and difference. The sound [of the word "all"] pervades all phenomena, and its nature consists of action (*karman*) and so forth.
This is a reason that is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) yet remains doubtful regarding the property-bearer (*dharmin*).

In relation to what is doubted—such as the cognition held by the proponent and the opponent regarding a kitchen or similar object—how can this be said to be a "doubtful means of proof" (*saṃśaya-sādhana*)? This is a general inquiry and response. Question:
The first part of the preceding enumeration states: "Because of doubt, it is not an example," pointing to cases such as "like a kitchen" and so forth.
Why, then, in examples such as "like a kitchen," does doubt arise? The answer is: based on the example itself, there is no doubt regarding the smoke; however, the cause may be interrupted.

Now, regarding the reason (*hetu*) within that which resembles the proof (*sādhanābhāsa*), there is the "uncertain simile" (*samdigdha-dṛṣṭānta*). Even if one does not harbor doubt [regarding the reason], there is still uncertainty.
As it is said in the section on "contradictory reasons of equal force" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*): "These two are also cases of uncertainty. The intended meaning of this response can be understood.
The commentary on this "contradictory certainty" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) of the other's inference intends to say:
although one establishes for oneself the aforementioned inference as a contradictory certainty, there are not two [independent] positions of self and other;
rather, if both self and other are true, it is because one refutes the other's position—which is not a valid establishment—rather than establishing a similar [position] oneself.

The meaning is as follows: "Contradictory certainty" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) must necessarily involve one [of the two] being for oneself, for another, or common to both. In this treatise, it refers to that which is common to both.
If both are true *sādhana*s for oneself, they fulfill the three characteristics (*trirūpa*) and establish their own respective theses.
If both are true *dūṣaṇa*s for another, they possess the three characteristics. Since the present case is said to refute another, neither of these applies; thus, it is established as a contradiction.
This is the section on "Certainty.

Regarding the statement in the commentary that among the various types of "uncertainty" (*anaikāntika*)—both specific (*asādhāraṇa*) and general (*sādhāraṇa*)—those that are specific and general uncertainties constitute the fallacy of uncertainty:

Question: Within the category of general [uncertainty], the reason (*hetu*) occurs within the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) of others; why is this not [simply] a case of uncertainty? Answer: Because it is not commonly accepted (*na sādhāraṇam iṣṭam*).

If that is so, it is not even commonly accepted with respect to its own dissimilar class (*vijātīya*); how then could it be an "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*) reason within the common [domain]? Answer:
If the five types of inference were to apply to their own dissimilar class, they would incur the fault of contradicting one's own tenets (*svasiddhāntavirodha*).
Regarding the phrase "because it takes that which is contradictory to its own property as its self":
for example, establishing a thesis (*pakṣa*) of permanence while it is contradicted by impermanence is called "contradiction of the thesis" (*pakṣavirodha*).

Using "the state of being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) as the reason while it is [itself] impermanent is called "contradiction" (*virodha*), according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Because there is absolutely no such thing as a non-contradictory [reason] reaching a thesis,” the term “non-contradictory” refers to a reason such as "being produced" or a thesis such as "impermanence," which is called non-contradictory because it is free from all faults.
The phrase "the same applies to contradiction with the property" means that the reason "being produced" would contradict the thesis of "permanence," as it establishes impermanence instead.
This is also not erroneous; thus, the same applies to the contradiction [of the reason].

Regarding the phrase "because the property established by the contradiction is neither determinate nor non-existent," this refers to the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*); it means that the thesis and the reason do not exist therein.
The commentary asks: "Regarding those called 'contradictory reasons' (*viruddha-hetu*), such as when a reason returns to the thesis itself or does not conform to the meaning of the reason.

The intent of this question is as follows: When two opposing tenets, such as "permanent" and "impermanent," are presented, and a reason is offered that contradicts them, it is called a contradictory reason.

Furthermore, when two reasons—such as "being produced" and "not being produced"—are mutually opposed and serve as reasons for their respective theses, they are termed contradictory. This is the question.

This differs from what preceded. Previously, the objection was raised by turning back the contradiction between the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*). The meaning of the response can be understood [from the commentary].
Regarding the first point, "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*): it refers to whether the self (*ātman*) exists or does not exist—that which is to be established.
Accordingly, its differentiation is established. However, when one posits the statement "I exist," the underlying intention is to establish a self (*ātman*); thus, does this not establish existence?

Therefore, it is said that "existence" and "non-existence" are the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) that are established by names. Nevertheless, the teaching differs slightly from that of the *Hetuvidyā* (Logic) when compared with the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*.
In the *Hetuvidyā*, based on verbal expression (*śabda*), inference (*anumāna*) is established; that which is restricted to its own essence is termed "self."

This is the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). For example, just as sound cannot be inferred upon a jar, the common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) established by the mind—which penetrates other things—is like the perception of impermanence and so forth.
These two types of objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa-jñāna*) are collectively termed "specific characteristics" (*svalakṣaṇa*).

In works such as the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, phenomena (*dharma*) are designated as "specific characteristics" based on their own essence (*svabhāva*), such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth. If a name expresses a common characteristic...

That which is not reached [by inference] is the object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Taken collectively, these are termed "one's own object" (*svārtha*). There are also specific distinctions: the former is based on the distinction between the restricted and the general, while the latter relies on the sequence of priority.

As stated in the Commentary: "In the case of establishing the thesis (*pakṣa*) that sound is impermanent, regarding the sound 'eternal' and so forth, it does not reach the nature of that [sound], etc."
Regarding the abbreviated presentation of the ritual procedures herein: among the permanent and the impermanent, there are respective distinctions;
furthermore, the non-permanent are mutually distinct from one another.
As for the couch and seat, they apply to both.
The Dharma Master says: This is likely an error; it should read "according to the accumulation" (*zhǔn jī*).

Regarding the commentary's statement that the eyes and so forth function solely as real *paranirmita-upabhoga* (enjoyment by others), while the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) function only as their provisional *parārtha* (benefit for others): [this refers to the distinction between the actual sensory faculties and the states of meditative absorption].
This immediately follows the reverse order to conclude the two preceding explanations.
Regarding the phrase "Seventy Verses on the Ultimate Meaning" (*Paramārthasaptati*) in the Commentary:

this refers to when the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, intending to refute [the views of] others, composed this treatise to critique the erroneous doctrines of other schools. It explains the *Suvarṇasaptati*.

Seventy [verses] explain the fundamental meaning and constitute the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*). Regarding the commentary on "that which possesses outflows" (*sāsrava*), there are two interpretations:

first, that matter itself can possess those afflictions (*kleśa*) which take it as an object; second, that the cognitive faculty (*ālambana*) which takes matter as its object possesses those afflictions.

It means "that which exists. Second, it is said that because karma is incited by afflictions (*kleśa*), it abounds within form (*rūpa*) and so forth; thus, it is "with-outflows" (*āsrava*) because it is produced by outflows.
The commentary states that there is the sound of "emptiness" (*ākāśa*).
Apart from the absence [of sound], there is no separate capacity [to produce it], because sound is not non-existent; thus, there is indeed sound.
The Commentary states that the concordant example (*sapakṣa*) likewise commits the fallacy of the unestablished reason (*asiddha-hetu*).
This means that because the reason is unreal (*asat*), neither the similar nor the dissimilar example can exist in relation to the synthesis (*sāmagrī*).
Since the category of synthesis itself is unreal, it is said that the probans (*sādhana*) is unestablished (*asiddha*).

"Existence is also not pervasive" means that there is a real cause of non-existence that does not pervade the property-possessor (*dharmin*). The proponent does not accept the existence of the property-possessor;

for instance, regarding the category of "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*), the opponent does not accept it as having the nature of existence—which is a reality that is not non-existent—within that conjunction. Therefore, it is said: [existence is not pervasive].
The cause is likewise not pervasive.
The commentary (*shu*) initially appears to suggest that [the cause] exists only where there is actualization;
yet, if one speaks of the existence or non-existence of a real cause, it seems to exist only within the context of the "real" category when the parents were originally in a subtle state.
The *Vaipulya* [sūtras] lack substantial reality; they cannot produce offspring, and so forth—each and every one is substantially real.

Since the Commentary already treats the "nature" that is devoid of a substantially existent nature as being of the same category as the property to be established within the thesis (*pakṣadharma*), [it follows that this is not a fault].
The meaning is as follows: The proponent’s formal inference (*anumāna*) states: "The property of existence (*sattā*) is not a substance (*dravya*), a quality (*guṇa*), or an action (*karman*).

This is the predicate (*dharma*) within the thesis (*pakṣa*). The proponent intends that this "not being a substance, quality, or action" is precisely the exclusion of [the universal] "existence" (*mahāsattā*) from substances.
Therefore, this "property of existence" is the property to be established (*sādhyadharma*).
Regarding the statement in the Commentary that the opponent’s position—that meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) contradict their own essential characteristics—is intended to mean the following:
apart from their substantial existence, with respect to the scope of what is merely intended, they exist as distinct designations;

thus, they are identical to being devoid of substantial existence. This contradicts their own intended meaning, for they lack the essential characteristic of substantial existence, and furthermore, there is no commonality with existent phenomena.

[The opponent] asks: "Does this not accord with [the principle of] identity and difference? Why does it not only contradict the existence of a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*), but also imply its non-existence?

[The respondent] answers: Because the existence of a real intrinsic nature exists solely as that which is admitted by the opponent; when one contradicts what is intended by that admission, the intrinsic nature itself ceases to exist.

This is not the same as the school that posits the eyes and so forth as being for the use of another (*parārtha*). For those who establish such a position admit the expression "for the use of another" within their own system. (8)
Regarding the true and the false: for now, one provisionally accepts the establishment of a true cause; however, because it conversely establishes the false, it is a cause of differentiation.
This is because it is the self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a partial phenomenon (*dharma*).
The commentary states that there is no quality (*guṇa*) and no activity (*karman*).

This is intended to clarify that Mahat (*mahat*) is neither a quality nor an activity. Regarding the phrase "based on the absence of subtle divisions," it means that its substance (*dravya*) is one, unlike [the categories of] similarity and difference which possess distinctions.
Regarding the commentary’s statement that “there is one [factor] which equally designates the cause of conditions”:

because the three—substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and activity (*karman*)—equally possess existence (*sattā*), they are termed “existent. Taking this as the cause, one gives rise to the cognition that conditions them equally.
This is like the *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) established by the Hīnayāna schools.

The meaning of the *Śāstra* (the Commentary) is that it admits that particularity (*viśeṣa*) constitutes the nature of the object-condition (*ālambana*), yet because it becomes distinct only upon reaching the expressive word, that [particularity] is not grasped [as such].
This refers to "sameness-and-difference" (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*).
Regarding the "existence" in the phrase "the existence of existence and non-existence," this has existed since the time of "sameness-and-difference."

This is the "existence" that consists of both existence and non-existence. The intended meaning is that the nature of existence (*sattā*) is precisely the nature of being an object of cognition (*ālambana*).
It does not mean that "existence" refers to a "Great Existence" (*mahāsattā*). Therefore, Pañcaśikhin established a formal argument (*pramāṇa*) to challenge this, stating:

"The nature of existence should not be something produced as a nature of existence, because it possesses the nature of being an object of cognition and is a single reality, just like the nature of similarity-and-difference (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*). This argument is necessarily cumbersome; however, if one were to add a modification, it would be stated as follows:

Regarding the fallacy of a reason that contradicts the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the subject (*dharmin*): it can only function as a contradictory reason for another party if that subject does not exist within one's own school.
Since the subject to be qualified is universally established (*prasiddha*), this fault certainly does not apply here. As for the charge of contradicting the other party:

because it would contradict one’s own school, [the reason] "having the nature of being an object of the cognition of 'Great' (*mahat*)"—though identical to "Great" itself—is separately established by distinct linguistic expressions denoting "sameness" and "difference."

This is established because "existence" (mahāsattā) possesses the nature of being an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). It does not take "sameness and difference" (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*) as its object-condition to serve as a qualification of the existent entity (*dharmin*);
this belongs to the ancient masters (*pūrvācāryas*).
Regarding the key points of the commentary's meaning: it is definitively established.

The *Yi* (義) states: "It functions as the nature of being a condition for both 'great existence' (*mahābhāva*) and 'non-existence' (*abhāva*). Because there might be a logical fallacy, it is omitted in the main treatise.
The *Shu* (疏) asks:
"As the proponents of phonology (*śabdavādin*) say, sound should not be produced, yet it possesses the nature of being a condition for sound, and so on, up to the differentiation of dharmas."
Regarding "contradiction" (*viruddha*):

the intended meaning here is that when the Buddhist doctrine posits the impermanence of sound in opposition to [the opponent], it constitutes a contradiction regarding the specific attributes (*viśeṣa*) of the subject (*dharmin*) for both the proponent of sound (*śabdavādin*) and the Buddhist doctrine.
Question: Does the Buddhist doctrine also implicitly accept that sound is the subject?

Regarding "nature" (*svabhāva*): the commentary explains that it is also admitted that sound has the nature of being an object of the ear. Furthermore, in the response, it says it "should not be struck or produced";
this is known by relying on this alone.
As for Master Shuguai, he was from Tangxing.
"Jifen" (即紛) is the name of the temple in Wencheng County. "Western River" (西方河) refers to what is called the Yiyifu (倚倚服) there.
Regarding "Sicizhou" (泀慈舟), the *Erya* states: "To go with the current is called 'yan' (沿); to go against the current is called 'su' (泝). "Liu" (流) refers to the flowing stream.

Regarding those who compose literary works that are disordered or deficient, they shall be executed by beheading. The official Yu Zhi considered that the first two characters [of the name] both carry the meaning of a bird in flight.
As for the phrase "the true cause is equal," the *Shuli men lun* (Treatise on the Gate of Discerning Principles) states: "It is solely due to the dharma."
Regarding the establishment of its dharma: the "initial dharma" refers to the causal dharma (*hetu-dharma*), while the "subsequent dharma" refers to the dharma within the thesis (*pakṣa*).

If one examines this response, it may at first glance appear not to answer the question posed. However, the underlying intent of the commentary is different. That interrogative phrase extensively elaborates upon the meaning of the reason;

the initial part provides a general explanation of the characteristics of the reason, while the subsequent part properly answers the question. This can be understood by reading it at length. Therefore, the following passage states:
It is said: "Therefore, these four reasons do not contradict the four [or six] [theses]. This is the formal conclusion of the answer.
Regarding the phrase in the *Śāstra* (Sūtra), "a distinct meaning upon the *dharmin*," the intent here is as follows:

when one states that "existence" (*sattva*) exists, this refers to the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the *dharmin*; however, the proponent’s intention is to establish it as distinct from the real entity (*dravya*).
"Great Existence" (*mahāsattā*) is the meaning of "distinction" (*viśeṣa*) upon the dharma; thus, it is designated as the "dharma. Question:

Since this is distinct from actual Great Existence, is it not rather a distinction of a dharma that possesses existence? How, then, can it receive the name "dharma"? [Answer: This is the point of contention between us.

Regarding the three characteristics of the thesis (*pakṣa*), these constitute the thesis established by the latter three reasons among the four types of contradiction. As for the remaining three [characteristics] of the thesis...

This refers to the other three types of reasons. Regarding the "establishment of the favorable reason" (*anuloma-hetu*) and the "direct refutation": these are the contradictory (*viruddha*) and the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) reasons.

As for "establishment," it means that the proponent brings forward their own thesis, which is the "correct" [position]; although it may occur in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), it is stated provisionally as a refutation.
As for "contradictory," this means that the opponent refutes the reason established by the proponent, such that the thesis becomes contradictory.
The commentary states that "it is therefore changed because it is a similar example (sapakṣa) established by the opponent" means that the Vaiśeṣika’s original similar example—
namely, "commonality" (sāmānya)— in their formal inference has been changed to serve as the dissimilar example (vipakṣa).
Regarding the commentary’s statement that "these four are not necessarily contradictory," the intended meaning is as follows:
it is not necessary for one reason to contradict all four [of the *asiddha* types] in order to constitute a contradiction; two or even three may also do so.

Regarding the commentary’s reference to what was previously explained as "non-establishment for both parties" (*ubhayāsiddha*), [it refers to cases where the reason is unestablished for both the proponent and the opponent].

With respect to this, compared to the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), neither the proponent nor the opponent accepts that this reason exists therein. How could one point to space as an example and say it is "produced"?

For both the proponent and the opponent, this would be unestablished (*asiddha*). Regarding the subsequent passage stating, "There are cases where both [parties] have the unestablished (*ubhayāsiddha*), and there is certainly no 'inconclusive' (*anaikāntika*) [reason]," this refers to the thesis (*pakṣa*);
it means that this reason does not exist upon the subject (*dharmin*) of the thesis, just as in the case of sound.
The nature of that which is constantly seen by the eye is precisely the absence of characteristics; thus, it establishes an inconclusive contradiction.
Since the initial characteristic must exist [for the argument to hold], yet the initial characteristic is not established, it is said that there is no inconclusiveness and so forth.
The commentary states: If there were no "limitless refutation" (aprasiddha), then these [fallacies of] the unestablished reason (*asiddha-hetu*),
the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), and the contradictory (*viruddha*) would all be cases where the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) exists in many instances within the thesis (*pakṣa*).
This immediately explains the aforementioned correct and fallacious reasons (*hetu*).
Regarding the statement in the Commentary that "only these five are established based on increase," the intended meaning is as follows:

among the establishment of fallacious examples (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*), those based on superior faults are established; since [the fault of] lack of application (*anupanaya*) is not superior, it is therefore not [included].

Regarding the establishment [of the thesis]: if one looks for a true analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*), the application (*upanaya*) and conclusion (*nigamana*) are not superior; thus, it is not established as a whole.
Because the "counter-example" (*vipakṣa*) is also not established—due to its being a superior fault—it is not established that there is no application or a reversed application.
Commentary: If one bases this on the argument that the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) are the logical reason (*hetu*), the intention here is as follows:
if one takes the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) as the concordant example (*sapakṣa*), this constitutes the fallacy of being "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*).
The rest may be understood accordingly.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “One [reason] is unestablished for one [party], up to the citation of the example: ‘The Buddha’s teaching does not admit that karma [is material],’” this refers to the opponent’s own school.

According to their doctrine, the two types of karma—bodily and vocal—are characterized by resistance (*sapratigha*). Based on this sense of the term “karma,” it also encompasses the three types of karma.
For the time being, we take up the fault of being unestablished for one party (*anyatarāsiddha*) as a single instance.
The commentary states that hesitation does not constitute [a valid response], as previously established; there are likewise two [types of hesitation].

Now, regarding the metaphorical illustration, there are also two [types], which correspond to the faults [of the opponent] and likewise possess four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*). Since the non-response is established by logical inference, it should now be clarified in terms of its explicit application.
Regarding the commentary’s mention of “the same example” (*samāna-dṛṣṭānta*):
this is known because it refers to other instances where the reason and the example are similar, as well as the phrase concerning the result of the mind.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that “if the reason to be established and the example are similar, the basis of the example depends on the reason and not on [other factors], etc.”: [this means that] when the reason and the example are concordant, the substratum of the example must correspond to the reason, and not to something else.
The intention here is as follows: since both the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) are capable of establishing the thesis (*pakṣa*), they are said to be "similar.
Furthermore, while the example relies upon that which is to be established by means of the reason, it does not rely upon the factual subject (*dharmin*).

The commentary states that when both the subject (*dharmin*) and the property (*dharma*) are unestablished, it means that both the capacity (the subject) and the object (the predicate) are individually unestablished.
Regarding the question, "Is it not the case that the thesis (*pakṣa*) is not non-existent because its distinct object is absent? [it is answered as follows].
This is a concluding statement. If there were no distinction [between the two], would this not mean that there is no thesis (*pakṣa*) at all?
As for the *Śūlī-dvāra* (The Door of Logical Analysis), it merely cites the existence of the basis (*āśraya*) of the example and so forth; it does not explain the dharmas in detail.
The meaning is clear: this is an elaboration while that was concise. Since the *Nyāyamukha* does not state either "non-existence" or "only," both [terms] follow the same principle;

if one is absent, the other is likewise non-existent. Furthermore, regarding the statement that "only this" serves to exclude existence and non-existence, this very treatise states both "existence" and "non-existence," whereby the four meanings are also established.
"Existence" refers to the first two cases where both [terms] follow accordingly; the remaining meanings can be understood by extension.

Regarding the statement that there are thirty-six cases where both the reason (*hetu*) and the thesis (*pakṣa*) possess an entity (*sattva*) yet neither is unestablished (*asiddha*), this refers to instances where,

with respect to a reason accepted by both parties (*ubhayasiddha*), there is an interpretation that it is not capable of being unestablished for both, whereas it is not the case that the reason accepted by one party alone possesses an entity.

It is likewise unestablished both for the common [opponent] and for the existence of the entity, and it is likewise unestablished for both non-existence and their combination. The fourth [case] is the reverse of this.

Regarding the statement that these are unestablished for both the common [opponent] and for the existence and non-existence of the entity, since four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi) have been formulated, the same applies to the unestablished nature for both self and other.
The remainder should be understood by analogy.

Commentary: Furthermore, regarding the statement that "there are two types of both-established and two types of established-as-equal, as well as non-existence," this intention clarifies that each of the preceding four positions contains its own set of four propositions. As for the first two, they admit only the basis;
the remaining [positions] each admit both existence and non-existence.
Regarding the commentary stating that "neither one nor both are established" when taking [the example] as a homologous instance (*sapakṣa*):

this clarifies that a certain class of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) asserts the existence of space (*ākāśa*) as something unchanging, yet maintains that there is no space in relation to the performance of action.
This means that for them, the reason is unestablished both for themselves and for their opponent.

Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* that "if there is mutual deficiency, neither is established," this explanation is based for the time being on examples where the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*) possess substantial reality (*dravyasat*). If it were applied universally, however, there would be a contradiction.

This is because, in order to refute the basis of cognition (*jñāna*), it is stated that "that which does not exist at any time is non-existent"; thus, although there is something established (*siddha*), it cannot be what is capable of being established (*sādhya*).
Regarding the lack of proof: if one follows this interpretation, the Master of the Commentary (*Sūshǔ*) would be admitting the existence of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Does the fault also apply if it is explained according to its specific divisions? If one follows the older texts, there is no such hindrance in the ancient tradition.
The *Śū* (Commentary) cites the ancient account of another’s rescue regarding sound, stating: "Even if it does not resemble the reason (*hetu*), it cannot be established.
This refers to Master Kuǐ’s account of the Prāmāṇika rescue of the preceding [position]. One should state: "According to your own *Saṃmitīya* school, sound is produced;

taking a jar as an example, it is produced by a staff and so forth. Sound is produced by the throat. Even though it does not resemble the reason of sound, it still obtains [the status of being produced]."

This constitutes a valid analogy. What prevents the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) within emptiness from serving as the reason for negating sound? Since the negation is fully established, it serves as a valid analogy.
The commentary immediately offers a rebuttal to this objection, stating that [the unconditioned] also succeeds as an analogy.
Regarding this, the Master [Kui]ji established his own position while refuting that of others.

As for the commentary’s point that, from the perspective of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), one should incur the fault of "non-establishment" regarding either one of the two [reasons] when compared to the Great Elements (mahābhūta) of the Mahāyāna—
this means that from the perspective of the Mahāyāna, it merely negates the fault of "non-establishment" regarding either one of the two [reasons] held by the other.
Regarding "neither [of the two] is established": since the four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) have already been formulated, the case where neither [self nor other] is established is likewise.
The remainder should be understood by analogy. As for "the reason (*hetu*) having one or the other [unestablished], as well as the basis being deficient":

This commentary on the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra* (Inmyō-so) was proofread by me at the age of nine in the ninth year of the Kyōhō era, the Jia-chén year, on an auspicious day in the fourth month, in accordance with my teacher’s command.
The characters in the old edition were not clearly legible, which caused me considerable doubt; thus, I appended my humble reflections to correct them.
Later, having examined other editions, I have scrutinized their accuracy and errors.
The general overview of this treatise is like [a map for] a traveler.
Now, in explaining this single treatise, I shall briefly establish three sections. First, the title of the treatise;
third, the analysis of the text through its divisions. Regarding the title...
The Buddhist scriptures extensively expound upon the causes and effects of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
Because they are internal to the path, they are called "Inner Science" (adhyātma-vidyā). Second is "Logic" (hetu-vidyā), which refers to the extensive exposition of the means of proof (sādhana).
A model for crushing the heterodox and manifesting the orthodox; through the clear causes of birth and realization, one accords with the profound principles of the True Doctrine.
Third is *śabda-vidyā* (the science of phonology), which refers to the classification of male voices, female voices, and those that are neither male nor female.

...and so forth. Some clarify the eightfold transformation of understanding, while others explain names through the six methods of interpretation; the extensive exposition of these various sounds is called *Śabdavidyā* (the science of grammar).
Fourth is *Cikitsāvidyā* (the science of medicine), which refers to the explanation of the causes of disease, the symptoms of disease, and the therapeutic strategies for healing;
hence it is called *Cikitsāvidyā*. Fifth is *Śilpakarmasthānavidyā* (the science of arts and crafts), which refers to the explanation of craftsmanship...
The methods of skillful arts refer to the systems and models of writing, calculation, seal-making, and arithmetic;

because this treatise extensively expounds upon these matters, it is called the *śilpakarmasthāna-vidyā* (Science of Arts and Crafts). This treatise is subsumed under the *hetuvidyā* (Science of Logic) among the five sciences (*pañca-vidyā-sthānāni*).
Second, regarding the explanation of the title of the treatise: this single work has two names. The first is *Hetuvidyā* (Logic), which is the general name for all such treatises.
The second is *Nyāyapraveśa* (Introduction to Reasoning), which is the specific designation of this particular treatise.
As for the "general name," it refers to the fact that, generally speaking, both Buddhist and non-Buddhist schools in the West [India] possess one [such system].
There are over one hundred treatises, all of which expound the principles of establishing and refuting arguments. They are collectively titled *Hetuvidyā* (Logic).

Although this is a specific name within the context of the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*), it remains a general designation for the science as a whole. As for the term *Hetuvidyā*, it refers to the "reason" (*hetu*).
For example, in establishing that sound is impermanent, what is the reason by which one knows it to be impermanent? Third.
The "equal cause" (sabhāga-hetu) is precisely because [the dharma] is impermanent. Furthermore, the term "cause" (hetu) refers to that which is depended upon;
this means that the principle of impermanence must depend upon a cause in order to be manifested. This is the wisdom that realizes the thesis (pakṣa).
This is because [the object] arises only when it awaits causes.
Now, when "cause" (*hetu*) is mentioned, two kinds of causes are indicated: first, the *parigrahahetu* (appropriating cause), which directly manifests the principle of impermanence;
second, the *janakahetu* (generative cause), which indirectly produces the knowledge that resolves the opponent's position.
The producing cause (*janakahetu*) and the revealing cause (*vyañjakahetu*) each have three types: namely, word (*śabda*), meaning (*artha*), and knowledge (*jñāna*).
The explanation of these three causes, as well as the clarification of their auxiliary and primary functions, is as described in the commentary; therefore, they are called "causes" (*hetu*).
Regarding the term "vidyā" (knowledge/illumination): according to the two Western commentators, one says that the cause (*hetu*) itself is the illumination; thus it is called *hetu-vidyā*.
This is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (possessive compound), because by means of the cause, the principle of impermanence can be revealed. The second says:
Because it clarifies the "cause" (*hetu*), it is called *hetuvidyā* (Logic). This is an example of the *tatpuruṣa* compound.

Within this tradition, there are two great virtuous masters (*bhadanta*) who each follow the Tripiṭaka and offer different interpretations. One says: "The knowledge of impermanent effects clarifies and understands the principles of the school;
because it is the 'clarification' (*vidyā*) of the cause (*hetu*), it is called *hetuvidyā*. Another says: "Impermanence is the correct... [text fragment ends].
The principle is fundamentally established; it is made manifest through the power of causes. Now, the school of Hetu (Logic) elucidates this, and thus it is called Hetuvidyā (Science of Reason).
To provide a comprehensive interpretation as a whole: the wisdom that realizes the thesis (*pakṣa*) is the clear understanding that brings about its establishment. This is what is produced.
The illumination of the *hetu* (causal condition) clarifies the principle of impermanence; this constitutes the illumination of the *pariniṣpanna-hetu* (perfected cause).
The illumination of the *vyañjana-hetu* (manifesting cause) clarifies the two fruits of manifestation and birth; this constitutes the illumination of the two causes of manifestation and birth.

Question: Since the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) can also clarify the thesis (*pakṣa*) and produce knowledge in the opponent, why is it not called "clarification by example" (*dṛṣṭāntaprakāśana*), but rather "clarification by reason" (*hetuprakāśana*)?
Answer: The reason (*hetu*) is the primary factor, while the example is its auxiliary. The name is given according to the primary factor; therefore, it is not so called.

This is explained by way of analogy. Furthermore, there is another interpretation: if one says that the *hetuvidyā* (logic of reasons) also includes those analogies, it is because both types of analogy are subsumed within the three types of reason (*trirūpa-hetu*).

If one says that the analogy clarifies [the reason], yet does not manifest the three characteristics (*trilakṣaṇa*), it is because the two types of analogy only discuss the latter two characteristics.
The phrase "entering into the correct principle" (*nyāyapraveśa*) is a specific name. "Entering" (*praveśa*) carries the meaning of skillful means for awakening and entry.
Regarding the term "correct principle" (*nyāya*), there are three interpretations provided in the *Hetuvidyā-ṭīkā*. The first states:
The great treatise on logic (*hetuvidyā*) composed by Dignāga is titled the *Nyāyamukha*. Why is it called the *Nyāyamukha*?
The Westerners explain it as follows: "Thesis" (*pakṣa*) refers to that which is established as the primary position and is revered as being correct.

"Reason" (*hetu*) refers to its underlying principle; it is the reason why that thesis is the correct principle. "Example" (*dṛṣṭānta*) refers to the gateway, because it is able to effectively reveal the principle of the true thesis.
Furthermore, another explanation states: "Wisdom" (*jñāna*) is the cause of correctness, derived from that correctness.

Because it explains the meaning of the three characteristics (*trilakṣaṇa*), the "meaning" (*artha*) is the principle (*nyāya*); because the meaning itself is the principle, the "words" (*vākya*) are the gateway (*mukha*).
Since they universally reveal the meaning, and because that treatise extensively elucidates the gateway of correct reasoning (*samyag-nyāya-mukha*), it is named the *Nyāyamukha*.
Now, Śaṅkarasvāmin, because the words and phrases of the *Nyāyapraveśa* were difficult to understand, composed this treatise.
If one studies this treatise, one will be able to penetrate the *Nyāya*. Because it is a treatise on the words and phrases [of the *Nyāyapraveśa*], it is said that "one enters into the *Nyāya*."
One explanation states: By studying this treatise, one is able to penetrate the correct principles (*samyak-nīti*) expounded in the Great Treatise on Logic (*Mahā-nyāya-śāstra*);
therefore, it is said that "one enters into correct principle."

One explanation states: By studying this treatise, one is able to realize and enter into the correct principles taught by all Buddhas—such as impermanence and emptiness—by means of the three characteristics of the logical reason (*hetu*);
therefore, it is said that one "enters into the correct principle."
This interpretation of both the general and specific names is the tradition of the Tripitaka masters from the Western Regions;
other interpretations are as explained in the *Śāstra*, and thus will not be described here at length.

"Sattva" is here translated as "sentient being" (yǒuqíng).
This means that for a bodhisattva, *bodhi* is the object sought, while *sattva* is the object to be saved; both names are derived from their respective objects.
Second, it is said: "Bodhisattva-sattvas" are so called because they take awakening (bodhi) as their object;
thus, they are named after both the fruit sought and the seeker itself. Third, "sattva" has the meaning of "courageous."
This refers to the courageous pursuit of bodhi; thus, it is named after both its object and its function.
In the current term "Bodhisattva," the two characters *ti* and *duo* have been omitted.
Regarding the second [point], the interpretation of the textual passage is explained in detail as set forth in the *Śāstra* (Commentary).
Since there is no omission in the *Śāstra*, I shall provide an auxiliary explanation: there are four types of "proof" (*sādhana*) as explained in the Western [tradition].

First, the "genuine proof," which refers to the three members [of a syllogism] being free from faults. Second, the "genuine and pseudo-proof," which refers to that which is contradictory... [text fragment ends].

It is certainly so. That which possesses the three characteristics in their entirety is called "valid" (*samyak*). That which contradicts the opposing measure (*pramāṇa*) is called "pseudo" (*ābhāsa*).

There are three types of pseudo-probans (*sādhanābhāsa*): namely, other types of inconclusive reasons (*anaikāntika-hetu*), contradictory reasons (*viruddha-hetu*), and fallacies of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadoṣa*), etc.
There are four types of pseudo-pseudo-probans (*ābhāsābhāsa-sādhanābhāsa*): namely, the four types of fallacies of the unestablished reason (*asiddha-hetu-doṣa*).
Furthermore, the reason (*hetu*) that pervades the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is precisely the primary element of the proof (*sādhana*).
If this characteristic is lacking, it constitutes a fallacy among the pseudo-proofs (*sādhanābhāsa*).
Now, when we speak of "proof," we refer only to the true proofs among these four; the latter three are all [pseudo-proofs].

Among those subsumed under "semblances of proof" (*sādhana-ābhāsa*), there are likewise four types of "refutations" (*dūṣaṇa*).
